title: Muslims in Britain
hook: a dome in Woking, a terraced house in Liverpool, sailors by the docks in Cardiff

segments.voice: Yesterday: enslaved African Muslims, like Omar ibn Said, who opened his own account with al-Mulk. Your line was they prayed in chains.

A domed mosque sits behind the trees in Woking, a quiet commuter town south of London. It's named for a woman far away, Shah Jahan, the Begum of Bhopal in India, who helped pay for it. Up north in Liverpool, a local solicitor named William Quilliam becomes Muslim, takes the name Abdullah, and opens a mosque in a row of ordinary terraced houses. Down in Cardiff, near the docks, sailors from Yemen and Somalia rent rooms, marry, raise children, and set aside a room to pray. No palace in any of it. Just streets, rain and neighbors. Today: Muslims in Britain.
screen: `A DOME IN WOKING.` → `A TERRACED HOUSE IN LIVERPOOL.` → `SAILORS BY THE CARDIFF DOCKS.`

segments.voice: One idea for today: Muslims in Britain are not a single arrival. They are many threads, woven over a long time. Some are converts, like Abdullah Quilliam in Liverpool. Some are sailors and dock workers, from Yemen, Somalia and the Indian subcontinent, who settled in port towns. Some are soldiers from India who fought in Britain's wars; near that mosque in Woking there is a burial ground made for Muslim soldiers. And then came families, from Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and later from Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, who came to work in mills, factories, hospitals and buses, and stayed. You can read that history in the buildings. Some mosques were built from the ground up with domes and minarets. Others began as a front room, a shop, a warehouse or an old chapel. On Brick Lane in East London stands a building put up as a chapel for French Protestant refugees, later a synagogue for Jewish families, and now a mosque. One building, three faiths, each praying in turn under the same roof. The Qur'an has a line that fits a faith carried to a cold, rainy island: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." For British Muslims, that has meant praying in a Cardiff boarding house, a Bradford mill, a Woking garden. The faith didn't wait for the perfect place. It found a corner, faced Mecca, and began.
screen: `NOT ONE ARRIVAL, MANY THREADS.` · `CONVERTS, SAILORS, SOLDIERS, FAMILIES.` · `ONE BUILDING, THREE FAITHS.` · `EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.` · then, large: `A LONG BRITISH STORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the mosque nearest you, or one you pass on the way to work, and wonder: what was the building before, who prayed there first, how did they find the money, the land, the patience? Then think of the first handful of people who unrolled their prayer mats in that place. If you pray, ask God's mercy for them in your own words; if not, simply hold them in mind.
Abdullah Quilliam, the Liverpool solicitor who became Muslim and opened one of Britain's first mosques in a row of terraced houses. Today's word.
Your line: a long british story. Many threads, not one arrival. Day one thousand twenty-seven, done.

howItsDone: British Muslims pray in a wide range of buildings, from purpose-built mosques to converted houses, shops and chapels, and some local mosques keep and share the history of the people who founded them.

chat.says: Did Muslims in Britain all arrive at once, in one big wave?
options: No. Converts, sailors, soldiers and families came as many threads over a long time.
Yes. They all came together in one wave to work in the mills and factories.
No. Most came only as students, then went back home once their studies ended.
